where.label: supported
where.says: Knossos lies about 5 km south of Heraklion's historic centre.
quote: about 5 km (3.1 mi) south of the city's historic centre

oldest.label: supported
oldest.says: Knossos is widely considered Europe's oldest city.
quote: Knossos is widely considered Europe's oldest city.

firstpalace.label: supported
firstpalace.says: The first palace was built around 1900 BC on a hill already occupied for millennia.
quote: The first palace was built around 1900 BC on a hill that had already been occupied for several millennia.

settle.label: supported
settle.says: Settlement on Kephala hill began around 7000 BC.
quote: Settlement on Kephala hill began around 7000 BC

westcourt.label: supported
westcourt.says: The West Court was a major approach to the palace and probably had ceremonial functions.
quote: The West Court formed a major approach to the palace and probably had ceremonial functions.

role.label: disputed
role.says: The palace is generally read as an administrative, economic, religious and ceremonial centre; its role as a royal residence is debated.
quote: the complex is generally interpreted as an administrative, economic, religious and ceremonial centre. Its role as a royal residence is debated.

size.label: estimate
size.says: The multi-storey palace covered approximately 20,000 square metres.
quote: The multi-storey complex covered approximately 20,000 m2

rooms.label: estimate
rooms.says: Knossos was a collection of over 1,000 interlocking rooms.
quote: Knossos was an intricate collection of over 1,000 interlocking rooms

quake1700.label: disputed
quake1700.says: The first palace was destroyed around 1700 BC, probably by earthquake, and rebuilt larger.
quote: The first palace was destroyed around 1700 BC, probably by an earthquake or a series of seismic events. The palace was subsequently rebuilt on a larger and more elaborate scale.

height.label: supported
height.says: The Second Palace period, about 1700 to 1450 BC, was the height of Minoan Knossos; the visible palace is largely from it.
quote: The Second Palace period, from about 1700 to 1450 BC, was the height of Minoan Knossos.
Its visible form largely belongs to the Second Palace period

d1450.label: supported
d1450.says: The palace was partially destroyed around 1450 BC; afterwards Mycenaean Greek influence grew stronger.
quote: The palace was partially destroyed around 1450 BC
After this event, Knossos continued to function, but with stronger Mycenaean Greek influence.

end1350.label: disputed
end1350.says: A major destruction by fire is conventionally dated to about 1350 BC; the final destruction is debated.
quote: A major destruction of the palace by fire is conventionally dated to about 1350 BC.
although the chronology of the palace's final destruction remains debated

linb.label: supported
linb.says: Thousands of Linear B tablets were found; Ventris and Chadwick's decipherment showed they record an early form of Greek.
quote: thousands of Linear B tablets
The Linear B tablets from Knossos were central to the decipherment of Linear B by Michael Ventris and John Chadwick. Their decipherment showed that the tablets recorded an early form of Greek

lina.label: supported
quote: Linear A, which remains undeciphered

magazines.label: supported
magazines.says: The west wing's long storage rooms held large jars (pithoi) for oil, grain, wine and other goods.
quote: The palace contained extensive magazines, especially in the west wing. These long storage rooms held large ceramic jars, or pithoi, used for storing oil, grain, wine and other commodities.

admin.label: supported
admin.says: Storage, recording and redistribution were central; records suggest the palace monitored farming, livestock, crafts and offerings.
quote: Storage, recording and redistribution were central features of palatial administration.
These records suggest that the palace controlled or monitored agricultural production, livestock, craft activity and offerings.

kalok.label: disputed
kalok.says: Minos Kalokairinos, a merchant from Heraklion, made the first known modern dig, exposing west-wing storerooms with pithoi; one article dates it 1878-1879, another 1877; Ottoman authorities stopped him.
quote: carried out in 1878 and 1879 for several weeks by Minos Kalokairinos, a Cretan antiquarian and merchant from Heraklion
Kalokairinos exposed parts of the west wing and identified storage magazines containing large pithoi.
The first excavations at the Minoan palace of Knossos on the Greek island of Crete began in 1877.
Three weeks later Ottoman authorities forced him to stop

court.label: supported
court.says: The palace was arranged around a large rectangular Central Court, probably used for ceremonies, gatherings and movement.
quote: Knossos was arranged around a large rectangular Central Court. This court was the organising space of the complex and was probably used for ceremonies, gatherings and movement through the palace.

wings.label: supported
wings.says: The west wing held magazines, the Throne Room complex, pillar crypts and repositories; the east wing, built into the slope, held the Hall of the Double Axes and the Queen's Hall.
quote: The west wing contained important administrative and ritual areas, including magazines, the Throne Room complex, pillar crypts and repositories.
The east wing contained elaborate rooms built into the slope of the hill, including the Hall of the Double Axes and the Queen's Hall.

light.label: supported
light.says: Light wells and shafts brought daylight and air inside; drains removed rainwater and wastewater; the hilltop caught summer sea breezes.
quote: allowed internal rooms to receive daylight and air despite the density of the building
Channels, drains and sloped surfaces helped remove rainwater and wastewater
the palace also received summer sea breezes

throne.label: disputed
throne.says: The Throne Room has a gypsum seat, benches, a lustral basin and painted griffins; Evans called it Minos's throne room; its function is debated, with ritual or priestly use proposed.
quote: It contains a gypsum seat set against the wall, benches, a lustral basin and painted griffins. Evans interpreted the room as the throne room of King Minos. Later scholarship has proposed other interpretations, including ritual or priestly use. The function of the room remains debated.

throneside.label: supported
throneside.says: The Throne Room complex is in the west wing.
quote: The west wing contained important administrative and ritual areas, including magazines, the Throne Room complex

gillieron.label: disputed
gillieron.says: Evans had the throne room repainted by the Swiss father-and-son artists Emile Gillieron; critics say some of its best-known frescoes were almost complete inventions.
quote: repainted by a father–son team of Swiss artists, Émile Gilliéron père and fils
some of the best-known frescoes from the throne room were almost complete inventions of the Gilliérons, according to his critics

columns.label: supported
columns.says: Minoan columns often taper downward, were usually timber on stone bases; reconstructed examples are among Knossos's most recognisable features.
quote: Unlike later Greek columns, Minoan columns often taper downward. They were usually made from timber, set on stone bases and finished with rounded capitals. Reconstructed examples are now among the most recognisable visual features of Knossos.

evans.label: supported
evans.says: The British archaeologist Arthur Evans bought the palace land with private funding, began large-scale excavation in 1900 and uncovered most of the palace.
quote: With private funding, he bought the surrounding rural area including the palace land.
In 1900, Arthur Evans began large-scale excavations at Knossos.
Evans uncovered most of the palace
the British archaeologist Sir Arthur Evans

minoan.label: supported
minoan.says: Evans established the name Minoan, drawing on the myth of King Minos.
quote: Evans established "Minoan" as the archaeological designation for the Bronze Age civilisation of Crete, drawing on the myth of King Minos.

recon.label: disputed
recon.says: Evans rebuilt parts of the palace in reinforced concrete; critics say this sometimes goes beyond the evidence.
quote: Evans undertook extensive reconstructions at the palace using reinforced concrete, colour and architectural interpretation. These works made the site visually accessible to visitors but have also been criticised because they sometimes go beyond what can be securely reconstructed from the archaeological evidence.

concrete.label: supported
concrete.says: Evans made extensive reconstructions using reinforced concrete.
quote: Evans undertook extensive reconstructions at the palace using reinforced concrete, colour and architectural interpretation.

unescorecon.label: verified
unescorecon.says: UNESCO notes the reconstructions are well documented and large portions of Knossos remain authentic.
quote: All reconstructions are well documented.
large portions of the site remain authentic

unesco2025.label: supported
unesco2025.says: In 2025 Knossos was inscribed as part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Minoan Palatial Centres.
quote: In 2025, Knossos was inscribed as part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Minoan Palatial Centres

frescoes.label: supported
frescoes.says: Many frescoes survive only as fragments; familiar compositions may combine ancient fragments with modern additions.
quote: many survive only as fragments and some published images are reconstructions
familiar compositions may combine surviving ancient fragments with modern additions

finds.label: supported
finds.says: Many of the most important Knossos finds, including fresco fragments, are in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.
quote: Many of the most important finds from Knossos are housed in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum. These include fresco fragments

northbull.label: supported
northbull.says: A stucco fresco of a bull is shown in the palace's North Entrance.
quote: This type of cattle motif is shown on the stucco fresco in the North Entrance of the palace.

bullworship.label: supported
bullworship.says: So many bull scenes were painted on the walls that Evans concluded the Minoans worshipped the bull.
quote: Painted on the walls of the palace were numerous scenes depicting bulls, leading Evans to conclude that the Minoans did indeed worship the bull.

bullfresco.label: disputed
bullfresco.says: The Bull-Leaping Fresco was on the upper storey of the palace's east wall; the leaper goes over the bull upside down; the technique and reasons remain obscure a century on.
quote: originally sited on the upper-story portion of the east wall of the Minoan palace at Knossos
the leaper goes over the bull in an upside-down position
the technique and the reasons for doing that remain obscure, a century after the discovery of the frescos

myth.label: legend
myth.says: In myth, Minos had Daedalus build the Labyrinth for the Minotaur; Athens sent youths as tribute until Theseus, helped by Ariadne, killed it and escaped by a thread.
quote: According to the myth, Minos ordered Daedalus to build the Labyrinth to contain the Minotaur, a creature with the body of a man and the head of a bull. Athens was forced to send young men and women as tribute until Theseus, helped by Minos's daughter Ariadne, entered the Labyrinth, killed the Minotaur and escaped by following a thread.

birth.label: legend
birth.says: In myth, Minos kept Poseidon's snow-white bull instead of sacrificing it; Poseidon made Pasiphae fall in love with the bull, and she bore the Minotaur.
quote: Minos prayed to the sea god Poseidon to send him a snow-white bull as a sign of the god's favor. Minos was to sacrifice the bull to honor Poseidon, but owing to the bull's beauty he decided instead to keep him.
To punish Minos, Poseidon arranged with Aphrodite for Minos's wife, Pasiphaë, to fall in love with the bull.
She then fell pregnant and bore Asterius, the Minotaur

tribute.label: legend
tribute.says: Accounts differ: seven youths and seven maidens every seventh or ninth year, or every year.
quote: Some accounts declare that Minos required seven Athenian youths and seven maidens, chosen by lots, to be sent every seventh year (or ninth); some versions say every year.

labrys.label: disputed
labrys.says: Some scholars link 'labyrinth' with the labrys, the double axe, but this is debated; the palace's complex plan probably shaped the Greek image of the Labyrinth.
quote: Some scholars have connected the word "labyrinth" with the labrys, or double axe, although this interpretation remains debated. The palace's complex plan, with its courts, corridors, staircases and multiple levels, probably contributed to the later Greek image of Knossos as the home of the Labyrinth.

evanslab.label: disputed
evanslab.says: Evans suggested the palace was the Labyrinth; Oxford geographer Nicholas Howarth says that idea must be treated sceptically.
quote: the complexity of the architecture prompted him to suggest that the palace had been the Labyrinth of Daedalus
Oxford University geographer Nicholas Howarth believes that "Evans's hypothesis that the palace of Knossos is also the Labyrinth must be treated sceptically."

coins.label: supported
coins.says: The Labyrinth motif appeared on the coins of ancient Knossos.
quote: The Labyrinth motif on Knossian coinage demonstrates the continuing connection between the city and the mythic memory of Minos, Theseus and the Minotaur.

unescolegend.label: verified
unescolegend.says: UNESCO says the legend of the Minotaur and the Labyrinth is directly associated with the palatial centres.
quote: The legend of the Minotaur and the Labyrinth is directly associated with the palatial centres

around.label: supported
around.says: Structures around the palace include the Theatral Area; the Royal Road linked the palace with the town.
quote: Important structures around the palace include the Small Palace, the Royal Villa, the South House, the Caravanserai, the Temple Tomb and the Theatral Area.
The Royal Road connected the palace area with parts of the surrounding town.

parts.name: Arrival
parts.stand: In the wide paved court on the west side of the palace, looking toward the ruins.

paras.t: Welcome to Knossos, about 5 kilometers south of the center of Heraklion. This hill is often called Europe's oldest city, and the palace in front of you was first built around 1900 BC.
Watch your step on the uneven old paving and stairs, and on a hot day, drink water as you go.

This open space is the West Court. It was a main way into the palace, and it probably had a ceremonial role too. In fact, what the whole building was for is a good question. It's generally read as a center for running things: trade, religion, ceremonies. Whether a king actually lived here, scholars still argue.

People were living on this hill long before any palace, from around 7000 BC. At its height the palace covered about 20,000 square meters, several stories high. One count puts it at over 1,000 interlocking rooms.

parts.name: A palace in layers
parts.stand: Stay in the West Court, facing the palace walls.

paras.t: What you see is mostly the second palace. The first was destroyed around 1700 BC, probably by an earthquake.

It was rebuilt bigger and grander, and that second palace was the height of Minoan Knossos. Around 1450 BC it was partly destroyed again. It kept going, but Mycenaean Greek influence grew stronger. A great fire is usually dated to about 1350 BC, though when the palace finally came to an end, archaeologists still argue.

The palace kept careful records. Thousands of clay tablets in a script called Linear B turned up here. When Michael Ventris and John Chadwick deciphered it, it turned out to be an early form of Greek. The older Minoan script, Linear A, still hasn't been read.

parts.name: The storerooms
parts.stand: Walk along the west side of the palace to where you can look down into the long, narrow storerooms.

paras.t: These long, narrow rooms are the magazines, the palace storerooms. They held huge clay jars called pithoi, for oil, grain, wine and other goods.
Storing, recording and handing out goods was at the heart of how this place worked. The clay records suggest the palace kept track of crops, livestock, crafts and offerings.

This wing is also where modern digging began. A merchant from Heraklion, Minos Kalokairinos, uncovered part of the west wing and found storerooms full of big jars. That was in 1878, or 1877 by another account. Ottoman authorities soon made him stop.

parts.name: The Central Court
parts.stand: Come into the big open rectangle at the heart of the palace and stand near its middle.

paras.t: This is the Central Court. The whole palace was arranged around it.
It was probably used for ceremonies, for gatherings, and simply for getting from one part of the building to another.

Get your bearings. The west wing held the storerooms, the pillar crypts and the Throne Room. The east wing was built into the slope of the hill, with fine rooms like the Hall of the Double Axes and the Queen's Hall.

Notice how the builders handled such a crowded building. Light wells and open shafts brought daylight and air deep inside, and drains carried away rainwater and waste. Up on this hill, the palace also caught the summer sea breezes.

parts.name: The Throne Room
parts.stand: Go to the Throne Room on the west side of the Central Court and look in at the stone seat.

paras.t: This is the Throne Room: a gypsum seat against the wall, benches, and painted griffins. Arthur Evans called it the throne room of King Minos. Was it? Scholars still argue.
There's also a so-called lustral basin. Some scholars think the room was used for ritual, perhaps by priests, rather than by a king.

Now look at the painted walls. After the dig, Evans had this room repainted by a Swiss father and son, both named Émile Gilliéron. His critics say some of the best-known frescoes here were almost complete inventions of theirs.

parts.name: Evans and the concrete
parts.stand: Find a spot where you can see one of the rebuilt columns.

paras.t: See how those columns get narrower toward the bottom? That's the Minoan shape. But what you're looking at is concrete: a reconstruction made for the archaeologist Arthur Evans.
Unlike later Greek columns, Minoan ones often taper downward, and the originals were usually wood set on stone bases.

Evans was a British archaeologist who bought the land here with private money and began digging in 1900. He uncovered most of the palace. He also gave this whole civilization its name, Minoan, after the mythical King Minos.

His rebuilding is still argued over. It makes the palace easy to picture, but critics say it sometimes goes further than the evidence allows. UNESCO, which listed Knossos as a World Heritage Site in 2025, notes that the reconstructions are well documented and that large portions of the site remain authentic.

The same goes for the famous paintings. Many survive only as fragments, and a familiar picture may combine ancient pieces with modern additions. Many of the most important finds, fresco fragments among them, are in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum in town.

parts.name: The bull
parts.stand: Walk to the North Entrance of the palace, where a plaster relief of a bull is shown.

paras.t: Bulls are everywhere at Knossos. Here at the North Entrance, a painted plaster relief shows one.
Evans found so many bull scenes on these walls that he decided the Minoans worshipped the bull.

The most famous is the Bull-Leaping Fresco. It was once high up on the east wall of the palace, on an upper floor. A figure goes over the bull upside down. How they did it, and why, nobody knows for sure, even a century after the discovery.

parts.name: The Labyrinth
parts.stand: Stay near the North Entrance, or find a quiet spot nearby.

paras.t: And now the legend. The story goes that King Minos had the craftsman Daedalus build a Labyrinth to hold the Minotaur, a creature with a man's body and a bull's head. Athens had to send young men and women as tribute, until the hero Theseus, helped by Minos's daughter Ariadne, killed the Minotaur and found his way out by following a thread.

Where did the monster come from? In the myth, Minos asked the sea god Poseidon for a snow-white bull to sacrifice, but it was so beautiful that he kept it. To punish him, Poseidon made Minos's wife, Pasiphaë, fall in love with the bull, and she gave birth to the Minotaur. Some versions say Athens sent seven young men and seven young women every seventh or ninth year; others say every year.

So was this palace the Labyrinth? Evans thought so. Some scholars link the word labyrinth with labrys, the double axe, but that's debated. And you can see how a building of courts, corridors, stairways and levels could grow, in Greek memory, into a maze. Not everyone agrees, though. One Oxford geographer says Evans's idea must be treated skeptically.
The link is old, either way. Ancient Knossos put the Labyrinth on its coins. And UNESCO says the legend of the Minotaur and the Labyrinth is directly tied to these palaces.

parts.name: Closing
parts.stand: On your way out, pause for a last look back over the ruins.

paras.t: Around the palace you'll find more of the ancient town, including the Theatral Area and the Royal Road, which linked the palace with the town around it.

Take one last look. Strip away the concrete and the legends, and what's left is people: people who stored their oil, kept their lists, and painted their walls with bulls. The monster is a story. They were real.
